concepts.name: Bethlehem
concepts.why: Name against passages: 'But you, Bethlehem' is Micah's address (and Matthew's quotation of it); Luke 2:4 and John 7:42 name Bethlehem but do not address it, and Luke 2:11 does not say Bethlehem at all ('the city of David'). Plain 'Bethlehem' is held by every remaining passage; Luke 2:11 is dropped. (Secular/Jewish reader: nothing else here asserts fulfilment; John 7:42 shows the crowd arguing the point, which is the right way to show it.)

Secular scholar / original arbitrates: 'the Son of God' in Mark 1:1 is absent from some early manuscripts, the same kind of textual question for which the drafter dropped John 1:18. Drop it for consistency; Mark 15:39 and Matthew 3:17 carry the Gospel's usage. Minor flag, not a drop: Mark 15:39's Greek has no article, so the centurion's words can be read 'a son of God'; the note is an exact BSB quotation, so it stands, but the concept should not lean on that verse. Psalm 2:7 and 2 Samuel 7:14 are shown whole (including 'When he does wrong, I will discipline him'), which is what a Jewish reader of the king's sonship would look for.

note_fixes: Isaiah 7:14: the note rests on the BSB's 'the virgin', where the Hebrew is ha-almah, 'the young woman'. Re-cut the note to the verse's words that do not depend on the translation: 'the Lord Himself will give you a sign … and will call Him Immanuel'. The verse itself is still shown in the BSB in the passage text, so nothing is hidden, but the site's own note should not stand on one translation's reading (secular and Jewish readers; the original arbitrates).
concepts.why: Secular/Jewish reader: the note is the site's voice and, as written, takes the Matthean reading of the Hebrew. The grouping itself (Isaiah 7-8 beside Matthew 1:22-23) is acceptable because Isaiah 8:8 and 8:10 are shown in their own setting (the flood over Judah) and Matthew says 'to fulfill' in his own voice.

Name against passages: only Colossians 1:15 and 2 Corinthians 4:4 say 'image'; Hebrews 1:3 is the near word ('exact representation'), but John 14:9 does not use the word, and reading 'seen the Father' as 'the image' is an interpretation (secular scholar; Reformed and Orthodox would also differ on what it unpacks). The brief names the image of God as a place the site must not take a side: this concept says only whose image Colossians and 2 Corinthians call the Son, and does not say what the image of God in humanity is, which is right. See the links note: it should link back to Image of God.

Secular scholar with Jewish readers in mind: the concept shows Deuteronomy 18:15, 18 and every New Testament use but not the Torah's own closing statement on the same figure. Add Deuteronomy 34:10 ('no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses') so the Hebrew Bible's own reckoning stands beside the New Testament's, and consider Deuteronomy 18:20-22 (the test of a prophet). John 1:21 (the Baptist's 'No') is exactly the kind of honest inclusion to keep.

Name against passages: Hebrews 7:24-25 says 'permanent priesthood' and 'intercede', not Melchizedek or 'priest forever in the order'. Intercession already has its own secondary entry. If a passage is wanted there, Hebrews 7:21 quotes the oath ('You are a priest forever') and holds the name.

Secular/Jewish reader, the strongest objection in this outline: the Servant in Isaiah is named Israel/Jacob repeatedly (Isaiah 41:8-9, 44:1-2, 44:21, 45:4) and 49:3 is kept, but without those verses the concept reads as if 'My Servant' were a single figure whom Isaiah 53 describes. Add Isaiah 41:8-9 and 44:1-2 (and 44:21) so the text's own naming is shown in full. Keep 49:5-6 as drafted: the text itself distinguishes the Servant who restores Jacob from the Israel of 49:3, and that tension should be visible, not resolved by the site.

Completeness and balance (secular and Jewish readers): in the Hebrew Bible the shepherd is first the LORD himself. Ezekiel 34:11-16 ('I Myself will tend My sheep', 34:15) is the immediate setting of 34:23, which the concept already holds, and Isaiah 40:11 and Psalm 23:1 say the same. Add Ezekiel 34:15-16 (Psalm 23:1 optionally), or the concept shows only the human shepherd.

Secular scholar and Jewish readers: Daniel 7:13-14 is shown without the chapter's own interpretation, 7:18 and 7:27, where the kingdom is given to 'the holy ones of the Most High' / 'the people of the holy ones'. Add Daniel 7:18 and 7:27 so the text's own words about who receives the kingdom stand beside the Gospels' use. Also add Psalm 8:4 and Ezekiel 2:1 (ben adam, 'son of man' as a human being, the Hebrew Bible's ordinary use, which Hebrews 2:6 quotes), or the name implies the phrase is a title everywhere. Note that the BSB's capitalised 'Son of Man' in Daniel 7:13 is a translation choice; the notes are exact quotations so they stand.

Completeness: 1 Corinthians 5:7 calls Christ 'our Passover lamb', so the New Testament itself points to Exodus 12; the concept's only Old Testament text is a simile in Isaiah 53:7. Add Exodus 12:3-7 (the Passover lamb), so the lamb the text names is shown, and so Jewish readers see the Torah's lamb and not only Isaiah's simile. Do not add Genesis 22:8 (no New Testament text links it; that would be the site's connection).

secondary_or_links: Links: add Image of God. Concept 14 is literally 'the image of the invisible God' and the drafter dropped the link on the grounds that the image is 'said of the Son'; but hiding an obvious textual connection costs credibility, and a link claims nothing. It is a neutral link that does not say what the image of God is.
Links: add Temple/Presence (or the theme that holds 'God with us'): Immanuel (Isaiah 8:10, Matthew 1:23) says 'God is with us' and the outline otherwise has no way back to the theme that develops it.

Secondary 'Name -> above all names' duplicates Philippians 2:9 already in concept 11. Fine as a pairing with Hebrews 1:4, but consider removing the duplicate so it is not a second telling of the same verse.

Last concept (34, 'In Him the nations will put their hope'): accepted as the theme's words of hope, and nothing dark is softened (iron scepter, judgment, despised and rejected, stone of stumbling all remain). One balance note for the Israel-and-church seat and for Jewish readers: the hope as drafted speaks only of the nations; the same oracle (Isaiah 11:10-12) and Jeremiah 23:6 speak of Israel. Add the sub-theme named under 'missing' before the last concept, so the final word is not read as hope for the nations in place of Israel.

Concepts 33 'Written about Me' and 11 'He will be called' were examined closely for a site-voice claim that Old Testament passages are about Jesus and passed: 33 holds only New Testament speech, in the first person and in each text's own words; 11 groups by the words 'called' and 'name', and Matthew 2:23's 'prophets' is the New Testament's own attribution. Everywhere else in the outline a New Testament text that links an Old Testament one (Luke 4:21, Matthew 1:22, Acts 2:31, Acts 8:35, John 19:24, 19:37) says so itself and is quoted as such. No concept name states or implies fulfilment in the site's voice.

missing.why: The texts plainly develop the gathering and safety of the people under the king (the same oracle as Isaiah 11:10, which the outline cuts at the nations; Jeremiah 23:6 is already in concept 11). Without it the final hope reads as nations only. Place before the last concept; keep it to the texts' words and take no side on how Israel and the church relate.

The best-known hope of the Hebrew Bible on this figure, the wolf and the lamb, was cut with Isaiah 11, and 'He will proclaim peace to the nations' (Zechariah 9:10) is the next verse after the one the outline quotes. Confirm the BSB wording of Micah 5:5 before naming the concept in its words.
The expected forerunner (Elijah, the messenger) is plainly developed alongside the Christ titles and is already visible in John 1:21 ('Are you Elijah?'). Jewish readers will look for Malachi 4:5.

'Jesus is Lord' is one of the New Testament's central titles and appears only in fragments here (Acts 2:34-36 under Psalm 110, Philippians 2:9-11 under 'He will be called'). Name it in the texts' words.

'Firstborn' is a title the texts give in both Testaments; Exodus 4:22 (Israel is My firstborn) and Psalm 89:27 (David) show its Hebrew Bible range, as the 'anointed' concept does for its word. Colossians 1:15 is currently cut off from it inside the image concept.
